job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

response.passage: When you kick a football, you apply a force to it, but the ball does not contain any force within itself. Once your foot loses contact, the ball continues to move because of its inertia, not because of a force pushing it forward. If the ball is resting on the grass, it is not free of forces; gravity pulls it down, and the ground exerts an equal upward normal force, keeping it stationary. When the ball hits a wall, the wall exerts a force on the ball, and simultaneously, the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. These two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other out. Even if a heavy truck hits a small car, the force exerted by the truck on the car is exactly equal in magnitude to the force exerted by the car on the truck. Momentum is a measure of motion, defined as the product of mass and velocity, and it remains conserved in all collisions, even when objects stick together after impact. An object in motion will maintain its velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force, meaning a constant force is not required to keep an object moving at a constant speed.
response.summary: Objects move due to inertia rather than stored force, and forces always occur in equal, simultaneous pairs. Momentum is conserved in all collisions, and constant motion requires no continuous force.

items.stem: Why does a football keep moving after you stop kicking it?

options.why: Student thinks the ball carries the force from the kick.
Student confuses inertia with a driving force.
Student believes constant force is needed for motion.
